title: Direct speech

objectives.can: Mark where speech begins and ends, and notice the change of verb forms inside it.

explanation.summary: Hebrew narrative has no quotation marks. A verb of speaking opens the speech, the speech runs on in the speaker's own voice, and the narrator returns with the next wayyiqtol. Inside the speech the verb forms change: commands, wishes, plans and statements about the present replace the chain of events.

sections.heading: How speech is opened
body: The usual opening is a wayyiqtol of the verb אָמַר, 'to say': וַיֹּאמֶר for a man, וַתֹּאמֶר for a woman. Everything after it, up to the point where the narrator resumes, is speech. Hebrew does not mark the speaker's words with quotation marks, and the English translation you see beside the text adds them.

Another opening is the infinitive construct לֵאמֹר, literally 'saying'. It follows another verb of speaking or telling and introduces the words themselves: in Genesis 22:20 the report to Abraham is introduced with וַיֻּגַּד לְאַבְרָהָם לֵאמֹר. Both openings can be used one after another.

A long conversation is a string of וַיֹּאמֶר clauses. Often the speaker is not named every time, and you have to follow who is talking from the sense, as in Genesis 22:7, where the same verb opens each turn of a conversation between father and son.

sections.heading: Where speech ends
body: There is no mark at the end of a speech either. It ends where the narrator's voice returns, and the clearest sign is a wayyiqtol of a new event with a third person subject: in Ruth 1:9 Naomi's blessing ends and the narrator goes on with וַתִּשַּׁק, 'and she kissed'. Another sign is a new וַיֹּאמֶר, which gives the floor to the next speaker.

sections.heading: The verb forms change inside speech
body: A chain of wayyiqtols tells what happened. Inside a speech, people do other things: they command, wish, plan, ask and report. The verb forms follow. The table lists the common ones with an example from the verses of this lesson. They are tendencies; the context decides.

The jussive and the cohortative are the forms of will. The jussive is a shortened yiqtol used for a wish or a command in the third person and, with the negative אַל, for a prohibition. The cohortative is a first person form, often with the ending -ָה, for 'let me' and 'let us'. The analysed text labels forms by this scheme, and in some verses the label of a wish is yiqtol and in others jussive. Later lessons treat the forms in detail.

head: Form
Typical use in speech
Example
rows: what will happen or what the speaker intends
what has happened, or a state now reached

sections.heading: Small words that mark speech
body: A speaker often addresses the hearer by name, a vocative, as in Genesis 22:11 where the angel calls out a name twice. The reply הִנֵּנִי, 'here I am', answers a call.

נָא is a small word that softens a command or a wish, 'please': it follows an imperative (קַח נָא in Genesis 22:2) or stands after אַל (as in Genesis 13:8). הִנֵּה, 'look', draws the hearer's attention to something. עַתָּה, 'now', marks a move to the present or a conclusion: in Genesis 22:12 the angel says that 'now' he knows.
Because speech is about the speaker's present, first and second persons are frequent. Narrative in the third person is rare inside speech, unless the speaker tells a story of his own.

misunderstandings: The English quotation marks in the translation are the translator's. In the Hebrew you find the beginning by the verb of speaking and the end by the return of the narrator.
A string of וַיֹּאמֶר clauses is not a repeated sentence. Each opens a new speech, usually of a different speaker.
The verb forms inside a speech do not tell a story. A qatal in a speech is often a present state ('I know') or a perfect ('I have gone'), not a narrative past.
נָא is not 'now' (that is עַתָּה). It is a particle of politeness or urging.

deeper.heading: Speech inside speech and speech to oneself
body: A character may quote another inside his own speech, and a speech may report what someone thought or said to himself. The same verbs of speaking are used for all of these. The only guide is the sense and the person of the verbs: 'I' and 'you' within a quoted speech change reference with the new speaker.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And Naomi said unto her two daughters-in-law: 'Go, return each of you to her mother's house; the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וַתֹּאמֶר opens Naomi's first speech to her daughters-in-law. Inside it, לֵכְנָה and שֹּׁבְנָה are imperatives in the feminine plural: 'go, return'. יַעַשׂ is a jussive, a wish with the Lord as subject. עֲשִׂיתֶם is a qatal, and it reports what the women have done for the dead and for Naomi.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And He said: 'Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt-offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: God's command. קַח, 'take', is an imperative, softened by נָא; וְלֶךְ and וְהַעֲלֵהוּ continue the commands. The yiqtol אֹמַר, 'I shall tell you', is in a relative clause and looks to the future. The speech is full of second person forms, and there is not one wayyiqtol in it.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abraham said unto his young men: 'Abide ye here with the ass, and I and the lad will go yonder; and we will worship, and come back to you.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Abraham to his servants. שְׁבוּ is a plural imperative. נֵלְכָה is a cohortative in the first person plural: 'let us go' or 'we will go'. וְנִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה and וְנָשׁוּבָה continue it. In Hebrew the speech does not say who is meant by 'we' except by the verb ending.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Lay not thy hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him; for now I know that thou art a God-fearing man, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son, from Me.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The angel's words. אַל with the jussive תִּשְׁלַח and again with תַּעַשׂ is a prohibition: 'do not stretch out', 'do not do'. עַתָּה, 'now', turns to the present, and the qatal יָדַעְתִּי says 'I know', a state reached at this moment.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And she said: 'Behold, thy sister-in-law is gone back unto her people, and unto her god; return thou after thy sister-in-law.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Naomi speaks again. הִנֵּה draws Ruth's attention to what has happened, and the qatal שָׁבָה tells it: her sister-in-law has gone back. Then the imperative שׁוּבִי, singular feminine, is the command that follows from it: 'return'.
